description:
What Happened to Alexa Internet? A Guide to Traffic and Competitor Research After the Shutdown

Alexa Internet, the website analytics service associated with Alexa.com, retired on May 1, 2022. If you landed here looking for an Alexa Rank subscription, that closure is the starting point for choosing what to use today. Alexa Internet was the company and service that measured web popularity. Amazon's Alexa voice assistant is a separate product. The SEO work people used to do with Alexa Internet can still be done, but the right instrument depends on whether you own the site, what kind of visibility you want to measure, and what decision the data will inform.

People sometimes remember Alexa Rank as a number that answered every question about a website. It was more useful as a rough screening signal. Someone buying advertising might have used it to compare publishers. An SEO consultant might have used it to put a rival site on a research list. A founder might have watched it change over time. Each person had a different decision in mind, and each one needs a different replacement. This guide walks through the decisions individually and uses a fictional example to show how the evidence fits together.

What Alexa Rank was useful for

A ranking makes a long list easier to scan. Imagine a developer choosing between several publications to pitch a tutorial. An order-of-magnitude idea of which publications had established audiences could help decide where to spend the first hour. The rank alone could not tell the developer whether the publication served the right readers, published tutorials, or accepted guest contributions. Those questions still required reading the site and speaking with its team.

The distinction matters more now that people sometimes compare numbers from unrelated platforms. A domain-wide popularity position, an organic traffic estimate, a daily count of actual site visits, and a Google search position describe different things. Converting all of them to the word ranking makes it difficult to explain what moved. If someone says a competitor ranks 300, ask for the source, period, market, and measurement. A website could be popular globally but barely visible on the specific search terms you care about.

Keep old Alexa figures when they explain decisions in a historical document. Add a note indicating where the data came from and when the service retired. A trend chart that continues past the retirement date needs a new line or a separate chart with the new source identified. The gap is useful context. It tells your audience why the successor data cannot be interpreted as a change in the old metric.

Start with the decision you need to make

Write down one decision before shopping for a replacement. A local retailer might want to decide which product page to improve next. An agency might want to compare three publishers before requesting sponsorship proposals. A nonprofit might want to determine whether an awareness campaign brought more people to its application page. These examples call for different evidence. A global popularity number is unlikely to resolve any of them on its own.

Define the unit you will measure. For a product refresh it could be visits to one page and the number of people who go on to request a demonstration. For a publisher comparison it could be readership in a particular country, supplemented by the publisher's own audience report. Pick the time interval. Daily data can help diagnose a sudden interruption. A monthly view often makes a better starting point for an editorial review because it reduces the influence of day-to-day variations.

Also define the consequence of a wrong reading. A small test advertisement is easier to reverse than a twelve-month sponsorship contract. For a low-cost decision, a plausible estimate and a quick manual check may be enough to move to the test. For a large commitment, ask for evidence the publisher can share directly and check whether its definition of the audience aligns with your proposed campaign. The quality of evidence should match the commitment.

Measure search visibility for a site you own

Google Search Console is a useful starting point for understanding how Google Search sends people to a site you can verify. Its performance report gives you clicks, impressions, click-through rate, and average position. Break the report down by page and query according to the question you want to answer. Website totals are often too broad to tell you what to change. A brand campaign can lift impressions while one product category quietly loses visibility.

Start with a set of pages whose role is clear. For example, a bicycle retailer could review its service booking page, its flat tire repair guide, and its page for replacement tubes. Filter each page individually. Read the search terms in context. Someone asking how to repair a puncture may want instructions. Someone searching for urgent bike repair nearby may want opening hours and a booking link. Both can land on similar pages while looking for different outcomes.

Interpret average position in context. A single number can cover different countries, devices, and queries. Review changes in impressions and clicks alongside it. If impressions increased on a group of relevant new phrases, the mix of queries may have changed. Looking only at the average could suggest the page lost ground while it actually became visible to more people. Compare like-for-like periods and use the same filters when investigating the underlying change.

Document what went into the report. Save the date range, page group, market, and any exclusions. Keep a note if the site changed domains, introduced a redirect, or moved content earlier that month. If an unusual change appears, inspect a small sample of landing pages and verify what visitors see. A report can guide you to the right URL, but it cannot inspect whether a button covers the page on a small phone or whether the excerpt promises an answer the article never gives.

Use first-party analytics to understand visits and outcomes

Search visibility explains part of the visit. Analytics helps you see what happens after a person arrives. If you operate the website, choose a few actions that represent progress. A service business might count completed inquiries and calls. A software site might count trial signups, then track how many new accounts reach their first successful task. Keep the event definitions accessible so another person can tell what counts and what does not.

Test these events using legitimate test activity. Complete the inquiry form and see whether the confirmation is recorded. Open the same page on another device and check whether ordinary navigation still works. If a change was made to a consent banner, analytics setup, or form provider, note the dates before comparing periods. A reporting change can make a healthy website look like it lost visitors. The opposite can happen when a single event begins firing more than once.

Search Console clicks and analytics sessions will often differ because they measure different events. Treat the series as complementary. The search report helps you investigate discoverability. Your own analytics can help diagnose whether visitors reach the action you care about. Compare both against a record of releases, campaigns, and technical changes. When the lines disagree, start with the page and the dates where the discrepancy is most obvious.

Suppose the repair guide received more clicks but generated fewer workshop bookings. Inspect whether the extra traffic came from readers outside the service area. Check whether the article gained visibility for questions about doing the repair at home. A guide can serve those readers well even if they never book a local appointment. Improve the guide for its audience and let the booking page focus on people who actually need nearby service.

Research competitors with estimated data

When you cannot see the competitor's first-party information, public observations and estimates can still guide research. Choose the tool based on the question. A search-oriented database can show terms and pages for further inspection. A market research tool can offer an estimated picture of audience size or channel mix. A backlink tool can help you find organizations that mention a competitor. Each source makes a different part of the picture easier to examine.

Make a small list of real competitors before paying for an extensive analysis. Start with four domains that compete for the same reader or customer. A local shop can learn from a national publisher without calling it a direct sales competitor. Add the publisher to a separate research list for examples of useful content. Then compare the local shops on page structure, geographic coverage, booking flow, and the questions their sites answer.

Keep comparisons inside one tool and one configuration. Record which country, date, and device category the report covers. Estimate comparisons are easier to interpret when the methodology remains consistent. Be careful with very small or new websites where a provider may have limited information. A blank field is a gap in the report. Visit the site, inspect its current pages, and look for reliable public evidence that helps resolve the question.

A practical outcome is a better research queue. If a competitor appears for several workshop pricing questions, inspect the page linked for those searches. Check whether it gives prices, provides examples, or explains how the business handles estimates. Ask your own service team which answers can be published accurately. Use the competitor page to identify the question, then build your own answer from your rates, services, and experience.

Compare potential publishers before buying advertising

Publisher comparison is a different use case. Start by describing the audience you need. A distributor of bike tools might want to reach independent repair shops in two countries. The biggest cycling magazine by total visits may reach mostly recreational riders elsewhere. Ask the publisher about geographic distribution, newsletter audience, typical advertiser placement, and the reporting it can provide. Read the publication to see how sponsorships actually appear.

Check that the numbers refer to the agreed format. A website can report monthly visitors while the proposed campaign consists of two newsletter placements and a short social post. For the newsletter, ask for a representative delivery and click report. For the website, ask how the proposed placement is measured and when reports are available. A small campaign with well-defined measurement can offer better evidence for your next purchase than a large package whose reporting is vague.

Set up a destination that matches the placement. If the advertisement invites a workshop to view wholesale tools, the link should open the relevant catalogue rather than your consumer homepage. Measure the actions you can verify and record the campaign dates before launch. Compare with the decision you wrote down at the start. If your goal was qualified inquiries, a high click count with few inquiries can prompt you to assess the offer, the audience, and the landing page separately.

Worked example for a quarterly SEO report

Assume a bicycle retailer wants to invest in one of three pages next quarter. Its service booking page had 6,000 Google impressions and 360 clicks in the previous quarter. In the current quarter it had 7,500 impressions and 390 clicks. Its tube sizing guide went from 9,000 impressions and 450 clicks to 14,000 impressions and 610 clicks. Its replacement tubes collection held steady near 4,000 impressions and around 200 clicks. The numbers are fictional and show how a report might be read.

The guide had the biggest growth, but the retailer should inspect the relevant query mix before assuming it deserves the next large investment. If many of the new searches ask for a conversion table, the writer could add one that reflects the shop's products and explains the units properly. The booking page tells a different story. Clicks grew more slowly than impressions. Review the device and search terms, the snippet and page offer, and whether a nearby location appears clearly. The right change might be a short improvement to the title and opening section rather than a complete rewrite.

Now add first-party context. Suppose the booking form generated 38 valid requests in the earlier quarter and 41 in the latest period. The retail team confirms that no tracking change occurred. The page has improved modestly, and the next step can be a deliberate test to see whether clearer workshop hours and a better booking link help. The other pages can still be maintained in small increments. Choosing one priority leaves time to measure the result before launching a second change.

Add competitor research as context. A rival lists examples of service times. A second rival offers an online estimate after a visitor chooses the repair type. These details show two ways to answer uncertainty about availability. The retailer can test a paragraph explaining typical service windows using its own booking records. If outcomes improve, record what changed and when. Avoid attributing every movement to one edit when seasonal demand or a local event also changed.

Build a report you can reuse

A useful template can fit on one page. State the business decision at the top, followed by the measured pages, the date ranges, and the expected action. For each site-owned metric include a sentence about what it measures. Put competitor estimates in a table labeled with the source, market, and dates. End with the experiment, its owner, and the date on which the result will be reviewed.

Keep raw exports with the report when they add reproducibility. Supply an editor with a one-line account of where the special cases belong. If a product page was redirected or the old site appeared under a second address, record that before importing new numbers. A future reader should be able to rerun the same comparison without guessing whether test traffic, international visits, or a retired URL was included.

Use consistent language in meetings. Say estimated monthly traffic when you mean a model output for another domain. Say Google Search clicks when the source is Search Console. Say bookings when a confirmed request reached your team. Clear labels make it easier for people to challenge an interpretation without turning the meeting into a dispute about which tool is correct.

Run the first monthly check without a legacy ranking

Set aside forty minutes for the first comparison. Spend the first ten choosing a result you can act on before the next review. A bicycle workshop could choose valid inquiries from its service page. Then use the next ten minutes to collect the smallest set of supporting numbers. Open the same date range in your search report and in your analytics. Record the exact page and the inquiries the workshop confirmed. Leave room in the report for the difference between an inquiry and a completed job.

Use the third ten-minute block to examine one change in detail. If inquiries fell, check whether it began on a particular date. Ask whether the team removed weekend slots, changed form fields, or stopped offering a service. Look at the page on a device your customers commonly use. A missing phone link or a message that appears after the form closes can be more informative than a change in a competitor's estimated audience.

Spend the last ten minutes turning the observation into a decision. Write down who will make the proposed change, where it will appear, and what evidence will be reviewed afterward. If the next step is to add opening hours above the booking button, describe what the previous version showed and retain a screenshot. If the change is too small to measure accurately after one week, choose a longer period and note how you will account for holidays or promotions.

Compare the new result with the earlier baseline only after checking whether the definition still holds. If the confirmation event includes spam this month, use the verified inquiry list or report the missing comparison. If the page received unusually large coverage from a partner, note the event beside the figures. A report that makes uncertainty visible gives the owner a better basis for choosing the next test.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get a new Alexa Rank for my website?

Alexa Internet retired the service in 2022. If your goal is to monitor current visibility, choose a measure you can collect today. For an owned site, start with your verified search data and analytics. For a comparison outside your site, choose a provider whose market coverage and definitions fit the work you need to do.

Is a domain strength score a replacement for Alexa Rank?

A domain strength score usually represents a provider's model for a specific purpose, often related to links or visibility. Read that provider's explanation before using it. If the project is about actual readership, test whether you can obtain a better indicator from a publisher's own figures or your own campaign performance.

Why do different competitors' traffic tools give different figures?

Each provider can use a different data sample, geography, time interval, and model. A search traffic estimate may exclude direct and referral activity entirely. Save the name and configuration of the tool and use those details when reporting a comparison. The estimate works best as one input to research alongside observations you can verify.

What should I keep from my historical Alexa reports?

Keep the dates, source names, and a short explanation of the decisions the reports supported. If you start measuring a new series, document the new source and first baseline date. Retaining the old documents can give context without asking the reader to interpret unrelated measurements as the same line.

Can I still compare sites with a small budget?

Begin with direct observations, public materials, and your own site data. Look at which pages competitors publish, how those pages answer questions, and what outcomes your pages produce. Pay for estimated competitor data when you know what evidence you need and how you will use it. That makes it easier to judge whether a subscription earned its place.

Google Search Console Performance report

For an owned website, compare Search Console data with your own analytics. For competitors, use traffic estimates as directional evidence.
